content.heading: 1.3 Vector Equations
content.paragraph: Important properties of linear systems can be described with the concept and notation of vectors. This section connects equations involving vectors to ordinary systems of equations. The term vector appears in a variety of mathematical and physical contexts, which we will discuss in Chapter 4, “Vector Spaces.” Until then, vector will mean an ordered list of numbers. This simple idea enables us to get to interesting and important applications as quickly as possible.
content.heading: Vectors in ℝ2
content.paragraph: A matrix with only one column is called a column vector or simply a vector. Examples of vectors with two entries are

where $w_{1}$ and $w_{2}$ are any real numbers. The set of all vectors with two entries is denoted by $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ (read “r-two”). The $\text{ℝ}$ stands for the real numbers that appear as entries in the vectors, and the exponent $2$ indicates that each vector contains two entries.1

Two vectors in $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ are equal if and only if their corresponding entries are equal. Thus $\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 4 \\ 7 \end{array} \right\rbrack$ and $\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 7 \\ 4 \end{array} \right\rbrack$ are not equal, because vectors in $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ are ordered pairs of real numbers.

content.heading: Geometric Descriptions of ℝ2
content.paragraph: Consider a rectangular coordinate system in the plane. Because each point in the plane is determined by an ordered pair of numbers, we can identify a geometric point$(a\text{,~}b)$with the column vector $\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} a \\ b \end{array} \right\rbrack$. So we may regard $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ as the set of all points in the plane. See Figure 1.

content.heading: Vectors in ℝ3
content.paragraph: Vectors in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ are $3 \times 1$ column matrices with three entries. They are represented geometrically by points in a three-dimensional coordinate space, with arrows from the origin sometimes included for visual clarity. The vectors $\mathbf{a} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 3 \\ 4 \end{array} \right\rbrack$ and $2\mathbf{a}$ are displayed in Figure 6.

image.alt: A graph depicts a vector and its scalar multiples enclosed within distinct cuboids in three-dimensional space.

content.heading: Vectors in ℝn
content.paragraph: If $n$ is a positive integer, $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ (read “r-n”) denotes the collection of all lists (or ordered $n$-tuples) of $n$ real numbers, usually written as $n \times 1$ column matrices, such as
The vector whose entries are all zero is called the zero vector and is denoted by $0$. (The number of entries in $0$ will be clear from the context.)

Equality of vectors in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ and the operations of scalar multiplication and vector addition in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ are defined entry by entry just as in $\text{ℝ}^{2}$. These operations on vectors have the following properties, which can be verified directly from the corresponding properties for real numbers. See Practice Problem 1 and Exercises 41 and 42 at the end of this section.

content.paragraph: One of the key ideas in linear algebra is to study the set of all vectors that can be generated or written as a linear combination of a fixed set $\text{\{}\mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,}\text{…}\text{,\,\,\,}\mathbf{v}_{p}\text{\}}$ of vectors.

content.heading: A Geometric Description of Span {v} and Span {u,v}
content.paragraph: Let $\mathbf{v}$ be a nonzero vector in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$. Then $\text{Span}\{\mathbf{v}\}$ is the set of all scalar multiples of $\mathbf{v}$, which is the set of points on the line in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ through $\mathbf{v}$ and $0$. See Figure 10.

If $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are nonzero vectors in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$, with $\mathbf{v}$ not a multiple of $\mathbf{u}$, then $\text{Span\,\,\{}\mathbf{u}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}\text{\}}$ is the plane in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ that contains $\mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{v}$, and $0$. In particular, $\text{Span\,\,\{}\mathbf{u}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}\text{\}}$ contains the line in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ through $\mathbf{u}$ and $0$ and the line through $\mathbf{v}$ and $0$. See Figure 11.
